source_spans.locator: Annual Review of Neuroscience 30, published p.535, Abstract: simple laboratory decisions share deliberation and commitment components

Annual Review of Neuroscience 30, published pp.539-541, Sequential analysis / Figure 2 / SPRT: successive noisy evidence is accumulated into a decision variable and sampling terminates at positive or negative criteria; bound placement determines sample requirements and error rate

Annual Review of Neuroscience 30, published pp.547-549, reaction-time random-dot-motion task / Figure 5: motion strength changes accuracy and decision time; diffusion fits account jointly for both; decision-related activity rises with evidence and approaches a common commitment level
Annual Review of Neuroscience 30, published p.551, criterion discussion: how the criterion is implemented neurally is unknown, while criterion setting controls the speed-accuracy tradeoff

conditions: two-alternative random-dot-motion decisions use noisy sensory evidence whose strength is varied across trials
population: macaque monkeys in the reaction-time random-dot-motion experiments reviewed by the source
task: discriminate net motion direction, report the decision by saccade when ready, and measure choice accuracy and reaction time across motion strengths
temporal_scope: momentary evidence is sampled and accumulated over deliberation time until a stopping criterion is reached

nodes.description: stimulus strength controlling the statistical quality of momentary motion evidence
noisy evidence sample bearing on the two motion-direction alternatives at a given time
running decision quantity formed by accumulating evidence across samples
positive or negative decision bound at which further sampling terminates and commitment occurs
probability or proportion of correct direction choices under a given evidence strength
time spent reaching commitment, reflected behaviorally in reaction time after accounting for nondecision latency
reaction-time random-dot-motion discrimination procedure varying motion strength while measuring accuracy and reaction time

relations.description: the distribution or mean strength of momentary evidence depends on stimulus motion strength
successive noisy evidence samples are integrated into a running decision quantity
accuracy and decision time depend on the stochastic accumulation trajectory and the criterion at which sampling terminates
criterion placement constrains the speed-accuracy tradeoff by changing how much evidence is required before commitment
the reaction-time discrimination probe exposes the joint effects of evidence strength on accuracy and decision time that are fit by the diffusion framework
